segments.text: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. In very simple words, it asks why people think, feel and behave the way they do, and it tries to answer that question through observation, measurement and evidence rather than guesswork.

This topic is the doorway to the whole subject. If an aspirant understands the major schools and perspectives here, later topics such as personality, learning, abnormal behaviour and health become much easier because those later topics repeatedly use the same basic viewpoints.

items.text: Definition and scope

: Learn psychology as a science of behaviour and mental processes. Its scope includes biological influences, cognition, emotion, learning, development, personality, social behaviour and applied areas. Do not reduce psychology to counselling or mental illness; those are only parts of the field.
Psychology as a science
: Scientific psychology uses systematic observation, testable questions, measurement, comparison and evidence. A scientific claim should be open to checking and revision when better evidence appears.
Early schools

: Structuralism tried to analyse conscious experience into basic elements. Functionalism asked what mental processes and behaviour do for adaptation. Behaviourism focused strongly on observable behaviour. Gestalt psychology emphasized organized wholes. Psychoanalytic approaches highlighted unconscious processes and early experience.
Modern perspectives

: The biological perspective looks at brain, nervous system, genes and hormones; behavioural approaches focus on learning; cognitive approaches examine attention, memory, thinking and interpretation; humanistic approaches emphasize growth and meaning; socio-cultural approaches examine social and cultural context. Modern psychology often combines levels rather than relying on only one.
Recent trends

: Contemporary psychology increasingly uses neuroscience, cross-cultural research, evidence-based practice, large datasets and interdisciplinary work. For the exam, understand the direction of these trends rather than memorizing fashionable terms.

blocks.text: From philosophical questions to an empirical science

segments.text: Psychology developed from older philosophical questions about knowledge, consciousness, free will and human nature, but modern psychology differs from purely speculative discussion because its claims are tested against systematically collected evidence. The field became institutionally distinct in the late nineteenth century, especially after Wilhelm Wundt established a laboratory at Leipzig in 1879. That date is commonly used as a milestone rather than as the claim that psychological thinking began suddenly in one place.

items.text: Scientific attitude

: A psychological explanation should be testable, open to disconfirmation and based on observable evidence. Researchers define concepts operationally, measure them as carefully as possible, compare alternative explanations and report enough method for others to evaluate the result. This is why a plausible story about behaviour is not automatically a scientific explanation.
Multiple levels of explanation

: Human behaviour can be examined at biological, cognitive, developmental, interpersonal, cultural and environmental levels. These levels often interact. Examination anxiety, for example, may involve autonomic arousal, learned associations, beliefs about failure, previous experiences, family expectations and the immediate examination environment.
Basic and applied psychology

: Basic research seeks to understand processes such as perception, memory or social influence. Applied fields use psychological knowledge to address practical problems in education, organizations, health, law and clinical care. The distinction is useful, but in practice basic and applied work often inform one another.

blocks.text: Historical schools and what each contributed

items.text: Structuralism

: Early structuralist work tried to analyse conscious experience into elementary components, often through trained introspection. Its methods were difficult to standardize, but the movement helped establish consciousness as a topic for systematic study.
Functionalism

: Functionalists such as William James emphasized what mental processes and behaviour do: how attention, habit, emotion and thought help organisms adapt to their environments. This encouraged broader study of real-world functioning rather than only the structure of conscious experience.
Behaviourism

: Behaviourists redirected attention toward observable behaviour and learning. Watson and later Skinner argued that environmental contingencies could be studied objectively. Behaviourism generated powerful learning principles, but strict versions were criticized for neglecting internal mental processes.
Gestalt psychology

: Gestalt psychologists argued that perception cannot always be understood by adding isolated sensations. People organize information into meaningful patterns, which is why the whole perceptual experience may have properties not obvious from its individual parts.
Psychoanalytic tradition

: Freud and later psychodynamic thinkers emphasized unconscious processes, internal conflict and early relationships. The tradition influenced clinical thought and culture, but many classical claims are difficult to test and do not have the same empirical support as modern learning, cognitive or biological findings.
Biological perspective

: Explains behaviour through brain systems, neural communication, hormones, genetics and physiological regulation. It is especially useful for topics such as sensation, stress, sleep and the biological vulnerability associated with some disorders, but biology does not operate outside experience and environment.
Cognitive perspective

: Studies attention, perception, memory, language, reasoning, interpretation and decision-making. It asks how information is represented and processed, and it provides mechanisms for explaining why the same external event can produce different responses in different people.
Learning perspective

: Focuses on how behaviour changes through association, consequences and observation. Classical conditioning, operant conditioning and social learning provide different mechanisms and should not be merged into one vague idea of 'habit'.
Humanistic perspective

: Emphasizes subjective experience, personal meaning, autonomy and growth. It broadened psychology's attention beyond pathology, though some humanistic concepts are harder to measure precisely than constructs in experimental psychology.
Socio-cultural perspective

: Examines how family, social roles, institutions, language and cultural norms shape psychological processes. Cross-cultural research shows that findings from one social setting should not automatically be assumed to describe all populations.
Biopsychosocial integration

: Many contemporary explanations combine biological, psychological and social levels. Integration does not mean listing three causes mechanically; it means explaining how influences interact across time and context.

blocks.text: Core research logic students should understand

items.text: Description
: Observation, surveys and descriptive statistics can show what is happening and how variables are distributed, but description alone does not identify cause.
Correlation
: A correlation indicates that two measured variables vary together. It does not establish that one caused the other because direction of influence and third variables may be uncertain.
Experiment

: An experiment manipulates an independent variable and measures its effect on a dependent variable while trying to control alternative explanations. Random assignment strengthens causal inference when it is feasible and ethical.
Replication and convergence

: Confidence becomes stronger when findings are reproduced and supported by different methods, samples and research groups. A single dramatic study should not be treated as final proof of a general psychological law.
Ethics

: Psychological research must balance scientific value with respect for participants, informed consent where applicable, privacy, minimization of harm and appropriate debriefing. Historical studies are useful partly because they led to stronger ethical scrutiny.

segments.text: Contemporary psychology increasingly combines neuroscience, computational methods, longitudinal research, large datasets and cross-cultural samples. At the same time, the discipline has paid closer attention to reproducibility, transparency, preregistration, open data where appropriate and the problem of overgeneralizing from narrow populations. These trends do not replace basic psychological principles; they improve the way evidence is produced and interpreted.

A useful examination principle is therefore to present theories as evidence-based models with strengths, limits and domains of application. Avoid writing as though one school permanently defeated all others. Modern psychology is strongest when mechanisms at different levels are compared and integrated.

rows: How do brain, genes, hormones and physiology influence behaviour?
How is behaviour learned from environment and consequences?
May understate cognition if used alone.
How is information attended to, represented, remembered and interpreted?
Mental processes must be inferred carefully.
How do subjective meaning, choice and growth shape experience?
Some constructs are difficult to operationalize.
How do social relationships and culture shape behaviour?
Avoid assuming group averages describe every individual.

items.text: Make a one-page timeline from early schools to modern perspectives.
For every perspective write three things: its central question, what evidence it uses, and one everyday example.
Take one behaviour such as examination anxiety and explain it from biological, cognitive, behavioural and socio-cultural perspectives.
Prepare a short comparison of “common-sense explanation” and “scientific explanation”.

rows: Avoid this error Do not write that one school has completely “proved” all others wrong. Historical schools contributed ideas, while modern psychology uses evidence from several approaches.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Start with a clear definition, explain psychology as a science, give a short historical development, compare major modern perspectives, add one simple example, and close by showing that present-day psychology is evidence-based and multi-perspective.
• Psychology is wider than clinical psychology.
• A perspective is a way of looking at behaviour; it is not automatically a complete explanation.
• Scientific explanations must be testable and supported by evidence.
• The same behaviour can have biological, psychological and social influences at the same time.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
